papers.title: Within-host evolution of an avirulent Salmonella vaccine strain reveals regulatory tuning of virulence functionality without loss of function
papers.abstract: Non-typhoidal Salmonella (NTS) relies on a costly epithelial invasion program encoded in Salmonella pathogenicity island 1 (SPI-1) to overcome microbiota-mediated colonization resistance. Because SPI-1 expression is a cooperative trait in which a minority of invasive SPI-1ON cells benefits the wider bacterial population, inflammatory infection models readily select for permanently avirulent "cheater" mutants defective in SPI-1 function. However, while frequently observed during acute infection, isolates from persistent human NTS infection rarely exhibit obvious SPI-1 loss-of-function mutations, raising the question of whether SPI-1 contributes to bacterial fitness beyond induction of acute intestinal inflammation and tissue persistence. Here, we addressed this question using a metabolically attenuated yet epithelial-invasive auxotrophic Salmonella serovar Typhimurium (STm) vaccine strain (STmAux) that persistently colonizes the murine intestine without causing overt inflammatory pathology or tissue infection while retaining SPI-1-dependent host interaction and immunogenicity. Following within-host evolution for up to five years, STmAux populations did not accumulate classical hilD or other obvious SPI-1 loss-of-function cheater mutants. Instead, parallel evolution repeatedly targeted the BarA/SirA two-component regulatory system, closely mirroring previous observations in persistent human NTS infections. Functional analyses demonstrated that evolved barA and sirA alleles tune rather than abolish SPI-1 function by sharply reducing the proportion of SPI-1ON cells while preserving their individual epithelial invasion competence. Reconstructed in a prototrophic strain background, early evolved isolates retained full intestinal and systemic virulence in vivo despite exhibiting strongly reduced SPI-1ON frequencies in vitro. Remarkably, identical sirA mutant alleles also emerged in a hilD-deficient strain background, indicating that selection for these adaptive variants is not contingent on canonical HilD-dependent SPI-1 activation. During prolonged evolution, additional mutations accumulated that were associated with loss of systemic virulence despite preservation of epithelial invasiveness, suggesting subsequent adaptation affecting host-interaction pathways beyond SPI-1-mediated virulence. Together, these findings identify regulatory tuning of the BarA/SirA control network as a conserved evolutionary trajectory during prolonged NTS persistence. Rather than favoring classical cheater-driven loss of virulence functions, long-term adaptation preserves substantial SPI-1-dependent host interaction while reducing the proportion of phenotypically virulent SPI-1ON cells.

papers.title: Structural signatures of salinity adaptation in Microviricetes capsids
papers.abstract: Phages, like their bacterial hosts, have evolved to proliferate across the full range of environments on Earth, but the specific amino acid residues that underlie their environmental adaptations remain elusive. Here, we developed a computational framework that uses structure-based multiple sequence alignments, a random forest classifier, and a phylogeny-aware regression model to find amino acid residues linked to specific environments. Applying this framework to public metagenomic data, we analyzed 1,110 Microviricetes major capsid proteins (MCPs) from the lake and ocean biomes, and found that ocean virus capsids were highly enriched in negatively charged residues on internal and external surfaces. This adaptation likely helps maintain solubility at high salt concentrations and stabilizes ssDNA-capsid interactions by sequestering positively charged ions inside the capsid. At intersubunit interfaces, ocean capsids showed enrichment of cation-{pi} and {pi}-{pi} interactions, which are more resistant to solvation than salt bridges and hydrogen bonds. Amino acid residues in lake capsids were more often substituted by biochemically dissimilar amino acids in ocean capsids than the reverse. Together, these results show that microvirus capsids adapt to high-salt environments through changes in surface charge and substitutions affecting intersubunit interactions. Further, we describe a general approach for studying the adaptation and stability of any protein family under complementary environmental or phenotypic conditions.

papers.title: A proteomics screen of HIV-1 ASP interactors reveals multifaceted effects on host cell homeostasis
papers.abstract: Nearly four decades after the identification of the HIV-1 antisense gene asp, the function of its protein product remains unclear. Evidence of ASP expression in vivo and the high degree of conservation of the asp gene among pandemic HIV-1 strains suggest a beneficial role for the virus. Using a mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics screen for ASP interactors, we identified nuclear, cytosolic, and mitochondrial host factors, congruent with variable sub-cellular ASP localization. A majority of the host factors identified in the MS screen are involved in pathways essential for host cell homeostasis, including DNA damage repair, intracellular protein transport, mitochondrial function and protein translation. Validating the biological relevance of these findings, we demonstrate that ASP shuttles to the nucleus to promote DNA damage repair and cell viability in response to genotoxic stress. We also finds that ASP promotes translation of mitochondrially encoded host proteins involved in cellular respiration and contributes to maintain mitochondrial membrane potential. Together, these studies identify ASP as a modulator of two major pathways of cellular homeostasis in infected cells, which has direct implications for HIV-1 persistence, spread, and the long-term survival of the viral reservoir.

papers.title: Moderately acid-tolerant Nitrospira strains obtained by single-colony isolation on plates
papers.abstract: Nitrospira are difficult to cultivate, and pure cultures are mainly obtained by dilution-to-extinction combined with other methods, a process that usually takes years to over a decade. Here, we isolated three Nitrospira strains from activated sludge and sediment within one year using conventional single-colony isolation. Pure cultures of two strains could grow and reform single colonies within 25-60 days on all three types of plates prepared with agar, agarose, and gellan gum. Phylogenetic and phylogenomic analyses placed them within lineage I and indicated that they represent potential novel species, with the provisional names Nitrospira monocolonialis for strain Z02 and Nitrospira limosa for strains Z47 and Z70. All three strains were moderately acid-tolerant, with a minimum tolerable pH of 5.0; strain Z02 showed the highest acid tolerance, retaining 74% of its activity at pH 5.5. Strain Z02 was also highly adaptable to oxygen concentrations of 1-21%, retaining 78% and 85% of its maximum growth rate at 1% and 21% O2, respectively. Compared with the representative lineage I strain Nitrospira defluvii, all three strains contain superoxide dismutase encoding genes and some unique genes. Comparative transcriptomic analysis suggested that strain Z02 upregulated genes involved in stress responses, cell envelope modification, and putative type IVa pilus systems under acidic condition. Overall, this study provides the first demonstration that Nitrospira can grow on plates prepared with common gelling agents and form single colonies within a short period, and that Nitrospira can also tolerate moderately acid conditions.

papers.title: Development of a core genome Multilocus Sequence Typing (cgMLST) and Life Identification Number (LIN) code schema for the Burkholderia cepacia complex
papers.abstract: Background The Burkholderia cepacia complex (Bcc) currently comprises over 20 closely related species; however, understanding Bcc population biology is complicated due to the continual advances in taxonomy and diversity driven by extensive horizontal gene transfer (HGT). Whilst there are conventional typing schemes for the Bcc, including Multilocus Sequence Typing (MLST), there remains a gap for fine-scale resolution typing of the species complex. Here, we present a 1,925 loci core genome MLST (cgMLST) and 14-digit Life Identification Number (LIN) barcoding scheme for the Bcc, that is embedded in the PubMLST database (https://PubMLST.org/organisms/burkholderia-cepacia-complex). Methods A dataset of 142 complete Bcc genomes spanning 19 species were downloaded from NCBI to develop the draft cgMLST scheme (Dataset 1). Two pangenome tools (PIRATE and PEPPAN) were then combined to give a consensus core gene list from Dataset 1. The 'core genes' from these outputs were then screened against the PubMLST loci, using a sequence tag scan, to identify their presence and curate new alleles. The core genes were then validated using a larger Bcc dataset (n = 934 genomes; 22 species) on PubMLST, which had been filtered for high-quality ([≤]200 contigs and 100% ribosomal MLST confidence). This refined the core gene list, ensuring a robust and reliable scheme using a threshold of 99% to classify the gene as 'core'. The population structure of the Bcc was subsequently analysed using the validation dataset to identify genetic clusters using ReporTree. Combined with statistical analysis, 14 allelic mismatch thresholds were identified for the LIN codes. Results The Bcc cgMLST scheme consists of 1,925 loci, which have been designated an arbitrary 'BCC' identifier. The cgMLST scheme and 14-threshold LIN code has been implemented in PubMLST and are publicly available for use. The Bcc genomes in the PubMLST database have been assigned cgSTs and LIN codes. Use cases of the LIN codes were validated using three previously published datasets, which spanned both outbreak investigation and phylogenomic lineage structures. Conclusions This stable, hierarchical LIN code nomenclature enhanced the ability to cluster isolates at multiple levels of resolution with examples overlayed on published datasets provided. The LIN code system is also backwards compatible with previous MLST and clonal complex (CC) nomenclature. Overall, the updated typing scheme will facilitate improve global public health through surveillance of the Bcc epidemiology including source tracing and outbreak investigation

papers.title: Preclinical Development of Enterobacter ludwigii LS57, a Human-Derived Swarming Strain, as a Live Biotherapeutic Product for Inflammatory Bowel Disease
papers.abstract: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) remains an area of major unmet need, and the undefined composition and manufacturing burden of fecal microbiota transplantation have motivated a shift toward single-strain Live Biotherapeutic Products (LBPs). Swarming bacteria are enriched in the stressed gut and limit mucosal damage, but no human-derived swarming strain has been developed as an LBP. We therefore report the complete preclinical development of Enterobacter ludwigii LS57, a swarming strain isolated from human feces. Chemistry, Manufacturing and Controls (CMC) covered a three-tier cell bank, 30 L fed-batch fermentation and a colon-targeted enteric-coated capsule, enabling consistent pilot-scale production. No treatment-related findings emerged in safety pharmacology (Sprague-Dawley rats) or in single-dose and Good Laboratory Practice (GLP)-compliant 1-week repeat-dose toxicity studies (Sprague-Dawley rats and Beagle dogs). LS57 was identified as E. ludwigii by 16S rRNA and whole-genome sequencing and produced metabolites with reported anti-inflammatory activity in culture. In Dextran Sulfate Sodium (DSS)-induced colitis, LS57 reduced weight loss, preserved colon length, lowered colonic pro-inflammatory cytokines and remodeled the gut microbiota. It also attenuated Trinitrobenzene Sulfonic Acid (TNBS)-induced colitis and enhanced the effect of ciclosporin A. In vitro, LS57 was non-hemolytic, non-cytotoxic, and acid-labile, formed no biofilm, and its resistance to aminopenicillins, cephamycins and imipenem was not transferable by conjugation. In vivo, LS57 colonized the inflamed colon without translocation in wild-type and interleukin-10-deficient mice, and experimental bacteremia was treatable with gentamicin or levofloxacin. LS57 combines efficacy across two mechanistically distinct colitis models with a safety package that addresses the principal regulatory concerns for LBPs, and a scalable manufacturing process, compatible with current good manufacturing practice, in which enteric coating overcomes the strain's poor gastric survival. These data support clinical development of LS57 in IBD.

papers.title: Effect of Lactobacillus postbiotic supplementation on intestinal permeability, nutrient digestibility, and gut microbial and metabolic profiles in aging cats
papers.abstract: Aging in cats is associated with declining nutrient digestibility and increased intestinal permeability, but evidence supporting microbiome-targeted interventions in older cats remains limited. We investigated whether daily supplementation with the Lactobacillus-derived postbiotic LB fermentate HF (LBHF) affected intestinal permeability, apparent total tract digestibility, gut microbiome composition, and fecal and plasma metabolomic profiles in older cats. Twenty cats aged 7.7-13.8 years were enrolled in a blinded, placebo-controlled crossover trial comprising two 29-day treatment periods separated by a 28-day washout; 18 cats completed both periods. Intestinal permeability was the primary endpoint, while nutrient digestibility, microbiome composition, and metabolomic profiles were secondary endpoints. LBHF did not affect intestinal permeability or absorptive capacity relative to placebo, although intestinal permeability was positively associated with age. Overall nutrient digestibility was higher during LBHF treatment, with the clearest endpoint-specific evidence observed for protein digestibility. LBHF was associated with a non-significant overall increase in Shannon diversity and a reduction in the relative abundance of Streptococcus lutetiensis. The increase in Shannon diversity was significant only in cats receiving placebo followed by LBHF, indicating a treatment-sequence-dependent response. Thirty-three plasma and 29 fecal metabolites showed significantly different changes during LBHF treatment compared with placebo. Plasma metabolites generally showed more positive changes during LBHF treatment, whereas most associated fecal metabolites showed more negative changes. Sequence-stratified microbiome and metabolome responses differed substantially, suggesting possible period, treatment-order, or carryover effects. Overall, LBHF did not improve intestinal permeability but was well tolerated and improved nutrient digestibility, particularly protein digestibility, while producing modest and sequence-dependent microbiome and metabolome responses. These findings suggest that the effects of LBHF in healthy older cats may relate more strongly to digestive efficiency and host metabolic responses than to intestinal permeability.

papers.title: Multiple adaptive trajectories shape antimalarial resistance evolution in Ethiopian Plasmodium falciparum
papers.abstract: Plasmodium falciparum malaria continues to impose a substantial public health burden across sub-Saharan Africa, with Ethiopia experiencing a recent resurgence in malaria cases. We analysed whole genome data from 120 P. falciparum isolates collected in 2024 across five ecologically and epidemiologically diverse transmission settings in Ethiopia and placed these in the context of 1,220 publicly available genomes. Parasite populations were highly structured within Ethiopia, while Horn of Africa isolates formed a genetically distinct regional cluster relative to East and West African populations. We identified evidence of recent positive selection surrounding the artemisinin resistance associated PfK13 R622I variant and detected co-occurrence with Pfcrt mutations together with recurrent selection signals at genes within the PfK13-associated haemoglobin endocytosis pathway, including Pfmca2, Pfkic7, Pfkic8 and Pfkic9. We further observed the emergence of the PfPX1 D384A-PIN haplotype, with shared identity-by-descent linking Ethiopian and Ugandan carriers, supporting a recent introduction followed by local selection. Widespread Pfhrp2/3 deletions occurred on diverse genetic backgrounds. Together, these findings reveal a complex adaptive landscape shaped by antimalarial and diagnostic selection pressures and suggest that parasite evolution in the Horn of Africa proceeds through multiple adaptive trajectories, rather than through the spread of a single dominant lineage.

papers.title: Women's health outreach using a rapid and fieldable Nanopore-based microbiome profiling workflow.
authors: N. P. W. C. J. van den Braak
papers.abstract: Background In recent years, scientific interest in the vaginal microbiome has increased due to its impact on women's health. Colonization of the Lactobacillus species in the vagina may contribute to protection against vaginal infectious diseases. In order to create public awareness regarding vaginal health and to provide insights into the vaginal microbiome, a rapid field microbiome analysis using Nanopore sequencing was evaluated at Lowlands, a three-day music festival in the Netherlands. This study aimed not only to evaluate a rapid sequencing workflow, but also to explore citizen science as a tool for health promotion and public engagement in women's health. Methods The workflow at Lowlands contained the following steps; (i) Dialogue concerning vaginal health, with invitation to participate. (ii) Informed consent and questionnaire to investigate knowledge on vaginal health, life-style and contraceptive usage; (iii) self-collection of a vaginal swab; (iv) DNA isolation using QuickExtract DNA extraction solution; (v) Ultrafast amplification of the 16S rRNA gene using NextGenPCR thermal cycling using 16S Barcoding kit 24 V14; (vi) Library preparation and sequencing was performed according to the manufacturers protocol using R10 chemistry; (vii) For data-analysis, MABA16S was used, with slight modifications. This workflow was established within 4 hours and results were communicated with interested participants.

papers.title: Northern palsa and peat ecosystem microbiomes are potentially supported by hydrogen and carbon monoxide metabolism
papers.abstract: Northern peatland and permafrost ecosystems are facing rapid changes, with increasing temperatures, permafrost thaw and shifts in hydrology. Characterizing microbial communities and metabolic potential from the soils and associated water bodies is crucial to understanding the changes in biogeochemical cycling in these ecosystems. For this, samples were collected and sequenced from subarctic palsa and peat soils, along with samples from associated thaw ponds and streams. Metagenomics was utilized in describing the microbiome and its metabolic potential in these environments. Palsa soils hosted microbial communities that were distinct from the peatland soils, ponds and stream waters. Soils and their adjacent ponds shared taxa, and peat soils and ponds also shared taxa with the streams, unlike palsa soils which were likely more hydrologically isolated. Based on metabolic marker gene ratio for denitrification [(nirS+nirK)/nosZ], palsa soils had the strongest potential to be a source of nitrous oxide (N2O) out of all the sample types. Marker genes for hydrogen gas (H2) and carbon monoxide (CO) utilization were abundant across soil environments and metagenome assembled genomes, suggesting that trace gas oxidation is likely one of the key energy sources for microbiomes. In the palsa ponds and peat soils pmoA, marker gene for methanotrophy, was the most abundant compared to the other sample types.

papers.title: Gene-resolved metagenomics reveals partitioned nitrogen transformation potential in a landfill leachate sequencing batch reactor microbiome
papers.abstract: Landfill leachate can contain high concentrations of ammonia and organic nitrogen requiring treatment before discharge. Sequencing batch reactors (SBRs) promote biological nitrogen removal through alternating aerobic and anoxic conditions, but taxonomic profiling alone cannot resolve how nitrogen transformation and competing retention pathways are distributed across microbial communities. This study applied gene-resolved metagenomics to a sludge sample collected from a UK landfill leachate SBR. Nitrogen-metabolism genes were linked to contig-level taxonomic assignments and metagenome-assembled genome bins to examine nitrification, denitrification, dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA), and assimilatory nitrate reduction (ANR). Nitrogen-transformation potential was partitioned across dominant and minor taxa. Nitrospirota and Pseudomonadota were the most abundant classified phyla, whereas Actinomycetota represented only 4% of the community but included Actinomycetes, which showed the highest within-taxon proportion of nitrogen metabolism associated genes. amoABC was assigned only to Nitrosomonas and Nitrososphaerota, whereas denitrification genes were more widely distributed but frequently occurred as partial pathways. nosZ was detected only in the minor phyla Chloroflexota, Acidobacteriota and Myxococcota. DNRA and ANR-associated genes occurred across multiple lineages; nirA in Nitrospira and DNRA-associated nirBD elsewhere within Nitrospirota suggested nitrifier-associated lineages may also encode nitrogen retention potential. Gene-resolved metagenomics identified candidate low-abundance contributors, restricted distributions of genes associated with ammonia oxidation and nitrous oxide reduction, and nitrogen-retention potential not apparent from taxonomic composition alone. Because the study examined DNA-level potential in a single sludge sample, expression, reactor chemistry and longitudinal data are needed to establish pathway activity and operational relevance.

papers.title: Functional Conservation Amid Extreme Divergence in Freshwater SAR11 Hypervariable Region 2
papers.abstract: The Ca. Pelagibacterales order (SAR11) is a ubiquitous bacterioplankton in aquatic ecosystems. The genomes of SAR11 bacteria contain hypervariable region 2 (HVR2), the largest HVR with extreme diversity. Previous studies collectively indicated the enrichment of cell-surface modification genes on HVR2, which have been hypothesized to facilitate phage evasion. However, characterisation of HVR2 has primarily targeted marine clades and been limited for freshwater SAR11 (aka. Fontibacterium). Here, we employed single-cell genomics and recovered 176 Fontibacterium HVR2 sequences from Lake Biwa (Japan) and Lake Zurich (Switzerland), across multiple sampling years for Lake Biwa. Comparative sequence analyses revealed that freshwater HVR2 showed high intra-population diversity and appears to evolve independently of the rest of the genome, mirroring patterns observed in marine counterparts. Nevertheless, highly conserved HVR2 sequence pairs were observed for distinct Fontibacterium species from the two intercontinental habitats, suggesting horizontal transfers of HVR2 with conserved functional configurations across divergent lineages and large spatial scales. Further comparison with 145 marine HVR2 sequences revealed HVR2 sequences displaying synteny between Fontibacterium and marine SAR11, and 209 gene families conserved across habitats, including three near-universally conserved families. All examined freshwater HVR2s contained initiator methionine tRNA genes concentrated near the boundaries of the 5S region, suggesting a tDNA-anchored integration mechanism. These results suggest the functional equivalence of HVR2 across marine and freshwater SAR11 clades, and the existence of a shared pool of HVR2 sequences that evolve reticulately through mutual genetic exchange, independent of the vertical inheritance of the rest of the genome.

papers.title: A global post-transcriptional regulator directs Acinetobacter baumannii carbon preference and gut colonization
papers.abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii is a multidrug-resistant pathogen that colonizes the gut, increasing the risk of subsequent infection and transmission. Recent work showed that A. baumannii catabolizes ornithine, a non-preferred carbon source, to colonize the gut. However, the mechanisms of carbon preference were unknown in A. baumannii. Here, experimental evolution identified the conserved RNA-binding protein CsrA as a regulator of carbon preference in A. baumannii, a previously unreported CsrA function. RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (RIP-Seq) revealed hundreds of CsrA-associated transcripts. A. baumannii CsrA directly bound and repressed expression of the ast arginine/ornithine catabolic operons. The Pseudomonas aeruginosa CsrA homolog RsmA repressed arginine/ornithine catabolic operon expression, suggesting this CsrA function extends to other bacterial taxa. Finally, CsrA was required for competitive fitness during A. baumannii gut colonization. These findings uncover a previously unrecognized role for a global regulator in A. baumannii carbon preference and persistence in the gut, a critical reservoir for multidrug-resistant pathogens.

papers.title: Viral replication and host response in airway epithelial cells predicts coronavirus pathogenicity and identifies HCoV-229E as an atypical seasonal coronavirus
papers.abstract: Human coronaviruses (HCoVs) range from mild seasonal strains to pathogenic viruses that cause severe pneumonia. The virological and host determinants that distinguish pathogenic coronaviruses (MERS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2) from seasonal strains (HCoV-229E, HCoV-NL63 and HCoV-OC43) remain poorly defined. To identify determinants of pathogenicity, we systematically compared replication, cellular tropism, innate responses and cytopathogenicity of pathogenic compared with seasonal HCoVs across nasal, bronchial, small airway and embryonic stem cell derived alveolar type II (AT2) epithelial cell cultures. All HCoVs preferentially infected ciliated cells in the upper airway, but only pathogenic viruses replicated to high titres in AT2 cells. Pathogenic HCoVs reprogrammed AT2 function and suppressed key innate immune signatures, consistent with distal lung epithelial dysfunction. In contrast, seasonal HCoVs were associated with limited alveolar replication and milder disruption of AT2 homeostasis. Strikingly, despite modest replication in all cell types, HCoV-229E induced pronounced epithelial injury, cilia loss and strong interferon stimulated gene expression, as well as induction of cellular stress/death programmes resembling those induced by MERS-CoV. These findings highlight the striking differences in cellular responses throughout the airways and between distinct HCoV strains and emphasizes the importance of assessing distal lung tropism and epithelial host responses to evaluate emergent coronaviruses to inform pandemic preparedness strategies.

papers.title: Characterization of Lactobacillus rhamnosus-Derived Extracellular Vesicles and Their Cellular Cytoprotective Effects Against Trimethylamine-Induced Oxidative Stress in Caco-2 Cells
papers.abstract: Dietary trimethylamine (TMA) underwent gut microbiota-mediated catabolism and subsequent hepatic oxidation to generate trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), a key metabolic factor linked to vascular and colorectal diseases. While the systemic effects of circulating TMAO were heavily investigated, the direct localized cellular interactions of its precursor, TMA, at the intestinal epithelial level required further elucidation. This study characterized extracellular vesicles isolated from Lactobacillus rhamnosus (Lr-EVs) and evaluated their cytoprotective potential in an in vitro human intestinal Caco-2 cell model under TMA-induced stress. Exposure to a high concentration of TMA (20 mM) significantly reduced Caco-2 viability to 78.8%, triggered intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, and compromised tight junction integrity as observed via the disruption of Zonula Occludens-1 (ZO-1) alignment. Co-treatment with Lr-EVs (100-300 g/mL) counteracted this cellular toxicity, enhancing cell survival up to 172%. Quantitative PCR analysis revealed that Lr-EVs suppressed the transcriptional upregulation of the pro-inflammatory gene IL-1{beta}, restored the expression of the metabolic regulator SIRT1, and stabilized transcript levels of key mitochondrial-encoded electron transport chain genes (ND6, CYTB, CO1, and ATP6). Additionally, Lr-EVs exhibited intrinsic radical scavenging activities in cell-free ABTS and DPPH assays. These preliminary in vitro findings demonstrated that Lr-EVs mitigated TMA-induced cellular injury, oxidative stress, and junctional disruption at the transcriptomic level, supporting further investigation of probiotic-derived EVs as prospective cell-free functional ingredients.

papers.title: Novel viral diversity and geographic structuring in the New Zealand West Coast blackfly (Austrosimulium ungulatum)
papers.abstract: Background Vector-borne diseases represent a major global public health burden, with climate change, land-use change and increasing human activity altering arthropod vector distributions and creating opportunities for infectious disease emergence. In Aotearoa New Zealand, insects commonly referred to as "sandflies" are blackflies belonging to the family Simuliidae. The West Coast blackfly, Austrosimulium ungulatum, is an endemic, human-biting species abundant throughout the South Island, yet its associated viral diversity remains largely unexplored. Methods Here, we used metatranscriptomic sequencing to characterise the virome of the West Coast blackfly and investigate patterns of viral diversity and community composition across geographical and environmental gradients. A total of 425 blackflies were collected from 19 locations spanning approximately 187 km. Results We identified 94 viral sequences across 16 orders and six phyla, all of which were putatively novel viruses. These included divergent lineages within families containing recognised vertebrate and arthropod pathogens, such as the Rhabdoviridae and Orthomyxoviridae. Viral community composition varied among sampling locations, but no significant associations were detected between land-use categories and viral diversity or community composition. In contrast, we revealed a weak but significant positive correlation between geographical distance and viral community dissimilarity, suggesting some degree of spatial structuring across the sampling range. Conclusions This study provides the first metatranscriptomic characterisation of the virome associated with the endemic West Coast blackfly, revealing substantial previously undescribed viral diversity and providing insights into the geographical distribution of arthropod-associated viral communities.

papers.title: Structural basis of virion assembly in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis-infecting mycobacteriophage SWU1
papers.abstract: The rising threat of drug-resistant tuberculosis has renewed interest in bacteriophage therapy as an urgently needed alternative. Rational engineering of these viruses, however, requires an atomic-level understanding of virion architecture. Mycobacteriophage SWU1 belongs to subcluster A2, one of the few mycobacteriophage lineages known to infect Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tuberculosis). Using single-particle cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), we resolved essentially the entire SWU1 virion architecture by localized reconstruction of four modules, the capsid, portal vertex, tail and baseplate, at resolutions of 3.62 [A], 3.51 [A], 3.70 [A] and 3.22 [A], respectively. The T=7 capsid comprises 415 copies of an HK97-fold major capsid protein and lacks any decoration protein in density. The 12-fold portal reconciles its C5-C12 mismatch with the capsid vertex through defined, non-equivalent subunit contacts. The baseplate carries a 13-fold tail-fiber ring on a 6-fold hub, a geometry without precedent among characterized phages, established here by symmetry-free reconstruction. These findings provide the critical insights into the assembly and infection of SWU1, laying a structural foundation for the future optimization of phage-based anti-TB therapeutics.

papers.title: Metagenomic Insights into the Fecal Microbiome, Resistome, and Mobilome of Beef Cattle in Cow-Calf Operations in Florida, United States
papers.abstract: Food-producing animals are a focus of One Health approaches to antimicrobial resistance (AMR) as reservoirs of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria (ARB) and antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs). We hypothesized that microbial composition, ARGs profiles, and mobile genetic element (MGE) profiles would differ by operation size and animal age group. Fecal samples from 162 cows and calves were combined into 54 composite samples, each comprising three animals of the same age group. Across operation sizes, Bacillota (51.4-64.9%), Bacteroidota (12.0-17.3%), Pseudomonadota (10.3-16.5%), and Actinomycetota (3.3-10.9%) were predominant phyla. Alpha diversity did not differ among operation sizes; however, cows exhibited greater observed richness, Shannon diversity, and Simpson diversity than calves (all P < 0.001). Microbial composition did not differ significantly among operation sizes (PERMANOVA, R{superscript 2} = 0.065, P = 0.609) but differed significantly between cows and calves (R{superscript 2} = 0.200, P < 0.001). Seventy-five ARGs representing 14 resistance classes were identified. Normalized ARG hit rates were higher in small operations (0.444) than in medium (0.278) and large operations (0.222; P = 0.088), whereas calves exhibited a higher estimated marginal mean normalized ARG hit rate than cows (0.383 vs. 0.247 hits/million reads; P < 0.001). Of 1,054 curated ARG hits, 23.9% occurred on predicted plasmid contigs, 0.9% on predicted viral contigs, and 7.1% on contigs containing insertion sequences. Overall findings demonstrate differences in fecal microbiome diversity and ARG abundance between cows and calves and indicate that predicted plasmids are associated with a notable proportion of ARG hits in Florida beef cow-calf operations.

papers.title: Mucin promotes pneumococcal colonization via autolysis suppression and tryptophan-mediated immune modulation
papers.abstract: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a leading human respiratory pathogen, yet its success depends not on disease but on its ability to persist as an asymptomatic colonizer of the nasopharynx. The nasopharyngeal mucosa is lined with mucus, whose heavily O-glycosylated mucin proteins are the most abundant macromolecules in the pneumococcal natural niche. While mucus is canonically viewed as a host defense barrier, we found that mucin actively reprograms pneumococcal physiology to promote colonization through two distinct mechanisms. First, mucin suppresses pneumococcal autolysis by specifically inhibiting the enzymatic activity of the major autolysin LytA, prolonging bacterial survival and restricting release of the cholesterol-dependent cytotoxin pneumolysin, thereby reducing host cell damage. Second, mucin induces de novo biosynthesis and extracellular release of tryptophan, an essential amino acid that humans cannot synthesize and that serves as a substrate for host immunomodulatory pathways. Tryptophan biosynthesis was critical for pneumococcal survival against macrophage killing, and its disruption abolished both colonization and invasive disease. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that tryptophan biosynthesis enables the pneumococcus to survive a bactericidal macrophage state while preventing macrophage transition to proliferative tissue repair. Together, these findings reveal that mucin is not merely a barrier but an active signal that reprograms the pneumococcus toward a persistent, host-tolerant state, identifying a distinctive repertoire of colonization mechanisms that allow a virulent respiratory pathogen to sustain long-term asymptomatic carriage in its human reservoir.

papers.title: Reversible decrease in swimming motility accompanies emergent β-lactam antibiotic resistance in Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) threatens global health, food security, and development; however, the evolutionary and molecular pathways that drive AMR remain poorly understood, limiting our ability to advance diagnostics and rapidly detect newly emerging resistance. In this report, we employed laboratory evolution of an environmental Escherichia coli strain (NIST 0056) under B-lactam antibiotic pressure (ampicillin and cephalexin) to specifically investigate the relationship between resistance genotype and motility phenotype. Within 10 passages, populations evolved varying levels of B-lactam resistance (including high-level resistance > 32 ug/mL) and showed consistent, dose-dependent reductions in swimming motility. Whole-population genome sequencing revealed large deletions in marR, SNPs in efflux pump gene acrB and fumarate reductase gene frdD, and mutations with evidence of amplification in the chromosomal class C B-lactamase gene ampC, collectively linking these efflux-mediated, B-lactam resistance mechanisms to loss of motility. Notably, motility reductions were more pronounced in individual clones than in the mixed populations (p < 0.005, Mann-Whitney; two-tailed test). Following removal of antibiotic pressure, motility was restored and AMR-associated mutations decreased in frequency, suggesting fitness costs associated with resistance. In aggregate, our results demonstrate that reduced swimming motility accompanies specific efflux-driven, B-lactam resistance mechanisms. Further work will investigate if the behavior is generalizable across flagellated Enterobacteriaceae. Because these rapid changes are amenable to high-throughput measurement, swimming motility may offer a tractable physiological metric for AMR detection in environmental surveillance.

papers.title: 41% of Gram-negative bacteria encode a Type Six Secretion System
papers.abstract: The type six secretion system (T6SS) is a highly studied, versatile bacterial nanoweapon that is important in bacterial pathogenesis and evolution. Despite extensive study, its prevalence remains poorly quantified. Analyzing 35,467 representative genomes, we find that approximately 41% of genomes in the average well-sampled Gram-negative genus (more than 30 sampled genomes) encode a T6SS. Further, we show that the distribution of the T6SS is patchy at all taxonomic levels. The uneven distribution we found is consistent with context-dependent selection, repeated evolutionary loss, or greater evolutionary lability. Our dataset provides a foundation for studying the drivers of T6SS distribution, and our pipeline enables similar surveys of other secretion systems, gene clusters, and multi-protein complexes across bacteria.

papers.title: Cell cycle progression and stalked cell morphogenesis in Caulobacter crescentus are regulated independently by the flagellum
papers.abstract: Bacteria colonize surfaces and form biofilms to survive in stressful environmental conditions. Many bacteria use an appendage called the flagellum to sense surface contact, and responding to these mechanical cues triggers rapid physiological changes to promote downstream attachment. Bacteria are known to secrete adhesins and alter their motility behavior to facilitate surface colonization, but these changes alone are insufficient to explain the breadth of adaptations observed in surface-attached cells. Disrupting flagellar assembly in the bacterium Caulobacter crescentus constitutively activates the surface sensing pathway, and this gain-of-function phenotype was previously used to identify a suite of flagellar signaling suppressor (fss) genes that promotes surface adhesion downstream of the flagellum. We show herein that a subset of fss genes also regulates the C. crescentus developmental program. Live-cell microscopy analysis of fss mutants identified independent sub-pathways that target stalked cell morphogenesis and cell cycle progression. We identify the predicted chemotaxis genes fssD and fssE as novel regulators of stalked cell morphogenesis and show that these genes act to stimulate the diguanylate cyclase PleD in flagellar assembly mutants. A separate pathway that includes the stator protein MotB and the recently characterized dNTPase FssC regulates entry into S phase downstream of the flagellum. We show that motB regulates cell cycle progression specifically in response to surface cues, and that stator-dependent cell cycle control occurs independently of c-di-GMP and CtrA. This work clarifies the downstream targets of the surface sensing network and establishes a comprehensive model for how surface sensing influences the C. crescentus developmental program.

papers.title: Integrated Transcriptomic and Translatomic Profiling Reveals Noncanonical RNA Junctions and Hidden Coding Potential in Porcine Epidemic Diarrhea Virus
papers.abstract: Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV) poses a major threat to the global swine industry. Although coronavirus discontinuous transcription is well characterized, the classical model cannot fully explain the diversity of viral RNA junctions, while conventional genome annotations may underestimate viral protein-coding capacity. To address these gaps, we integrated time-resolved RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), cycloheximide (CHX)- and harringtonine (HAR)-treated ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq), comparative genomics, and peptide mass spectrometry to investigate PEDV RNA expression and hidden coding potential. RNA-seq revealed that, at 3 hours post-infection (hpi), the 3 genomic region exhibited strong relative coverage enrichment, whereas the relative contribution of the 5 replicase-coding region increased rapidly between 3 and 5 hpi, suggesting a possible transition from sgRNA-dominated RNA accumulation toward enhanced genomic RNA replication. Genome-wide junction analysis identified 43,635 distinct noncanonical RNA junctions, although canonical sgRNA junctions accounted for 95.5% of all junction-supporting reads. Several abundant noncanonical sgRNAs were predicted to generate novel coding products, including N-x4, N-x2, M-x3, and M-x2, short peptides encoded within the 3 untranslated region (UTR), and two distinct N-terminally truncated S proteins, thereby expanding the potential coding repertoire of PEDV. Genome-wide reading-frame analysis uncovered a pronounced asymmetry in hidden coding potential, identifying 68 overlapping open reading frames (ORFs) longer than 40 amino acids in the +1 reading frame, compared with only three in the +2 frame. Ribo-seq further revealed a progressive redistribution of viral ribosome occupancy toward structural protein-coding regions during the later stages of infection. By integrating HAR-associated translation initiation-site enrichment with CHX-based ORF-level translation analysis, we identified several noncanonical ORFs with strong translation-associated evidence, including N-x1, N-x2, S-x1, and ORF1b-x13. Moreover, peptide mass spectrometry detected a characteristic peptide corresponding to N-x1 in infected samples, providing independent proteomic evidence for the expression of this previously unannotated viral protein. Together, these findings uncover extensive noncanonical RNA synthesis and hidden protein-coding capacity in PEDV, establishing a foundation for understanding novel viral gene expression strategies and their potential evolutionary and pathogenic significance.

papers.title: Diverse bacteria exhibit superadditive growth on mixed classes of carbon sources
papers.abstract: Heterotrophic bacteria in nature encounter complex mixtures of functionally-distinct carbon sources, yet whether such diversity enhances growth yield across diverse taxa remains unknown. We grew dozens of strains from four phyla on defined mixtures representing five classes of carbon sources. Remarkably, many but not all strains exhibited superadditive growth on a dilute mixture of all 64 compounds--that is, yield exceeding the weighted sum of yields on more concentrated subsets of functionally-similar compounds. Using exometabolomics, pooled genetic screens, and proteomics, we find that superadditive growth is associated with enhanced carbon consumption in the mixed-class medium, combined with reduced dependence on amino acid and nucleotide biosynthesis. Moreover, superadditive growth was predictable from genomes within the tested strain panel and correlated with genomically encoded sugar-over-acid preference. These findings reveal a previously underrecognized axis of physiological variation among heterotrophs and open the door to understanding the biochemical and evolutionary basis of this divergence.

papers.title: Thienothiazolocarboxamides: rapidly cidal agents causing catastrophic thiol collapse in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
papers.abstract: Thienothiazolocarboxamides (TTCs) were discovered as a hit in a whole cell screen for new antituberculosis agents. These molecules were rapidly cidal under both replicating and non-replicating conditions and killed Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) in macrophages. The heterobicyclic core of this scaffold was essential for activity and resistance to these agents was mediated by loss of EthA, a flavin containing monooxygenase also responsible for the bioactivation of ethionamide. EthA-mediated activation of TTCs in whole cells was found to produce mycothiol adducts and RNAseq profiles revealed a mechanism of action identical to the fungal mycotoxins patulin and nidulalin A. EthA oxidizes the sulfur of the thiazole ring to create a relatively stable sulfenic acid that reacts with cellular thiols. This unique, replication-independent, mechanism suggests the possibility that these molecules may contribute significantly to shortening the duration of tuberculosis chemotherapy.

papers.title: The role of Plasmodium falciparum acyl-coenzyme A synthetase 10 in fatty acid acquisition and lipid synthesis
papers.abstract: During the asexual blood stage, malaria parasites synthesize large quantities of lipids to support their rapid proliferation. Exogenous fatty acids obtained from host plasma are activated for lipid synthesis by parasite acyl-coenzyme A synthetases (ACSs). Of the twelve Plasmodium falciparum ACS homologs, ACS10 has emerged as a key blood-stage enzyme. Here, we sought to define the role of ACS10 in fatty acid acquisition and lipid synthesis during asexual development. To accomplish this, we have employed fatty acid alkyne probes of parasite lipid synthesis together with selective depletion of ACS10 in a conditional knockdown parasite line. This approach revealed that ACS10 is required for efficient incorporation of 16- to 20-carbon unsaturated fatty acid alkynes and a 20-carbon, saturated fatty acid alkyne into the major parasite phospholipids and neutral lipids. In contrast, shorter saturated fatty acid alkynes were either unaffected by ACS10 depletion or were hyper-incorporated into parasite lipids. ACS10 knockdown elicited a profound deformation of the food vacuole, which was likely caused by an imbalance of saturated and unsaturated fatty acids in parasite lipids. To promote the discovery and characterization of ACS inhibitors, we have established a fatty acid alkyne-based approach for identifying compounds that target ACS10 as their primary mode of action.

papers.title: SPARK: Systematic Profiling of Antibiotic-Phage Response Kinetics
papers.abstract: Phage therapy is, in practice, combination therapy: phage are almost always added to an ongoing antibiotic regimen, yet the combination is rarely designed to have a specific interaction pattern. Interactions can be antagonistic, additive or synergistic and cannot be inferred from either agent alone. Here we introduce SPARK, a method which quantifies phage antibiotic interaction from growth curves as the integrated deviation of observed growth from the growth expected under Bliss independence. We profiled 42 combinations spanning the ESKAPE pathogens and Escherichia coli with twelve antibiotics. We show that i) synergy and antagonism are resolvable within a single high-throughput assay, with the interaction determined by the phage antibiotic bacteria pairing; ii) 21 clinical Staphylococcus aureus isolates differ among themselves as widely as the seven species do; and, iii) interactions change between a few hours and two days, several reversing direction. Overall, SPARK needs only a plate reader and the analysis is performed with a specific openly available web tool.

papers.title: MmuPV1 and HPV E6 Elevate Nuclear Accumulation of IKK? to Impair NF-κB Signaling to Promote Persistent Infection
papers.abstract: The mouse papillomavirus (MmuPV1) E6 oncoprotein is essential for persistent infection and cancer development. Previous studies identified amino acid R130 of MmuPV1 E6 as critical for its interaction with the tumor suppressor MAML1. Mutation of this residue (R130A) disrupts MAML1 binding and prevents disease development in mice. In this study, we demonstrate that MmuPV1 E6 also disrupts NF-{kappa}B signaling through interactions with proteins in the I{kappa}B kinase (IKK) complex. Specifically, the MmuPV1 E6R130A mutant is defective in binding IKK complex proteins and fails to impair NF-{kappa}B signaling in mouse keratinocytes, suggesting that these interactions are necessary for E6-mediated disruption of this pathway. Furthermore, MmuPV1 E6 expression is associated with increased nuclear localization of IKK?, whereas cells expressing the E6R130A mutant exhibit no such increase. These findings suggest that E6-mediated nuclear localization of IKK? depends on its interaction with IKK complex proteins. Importantly, we demonstrate that the human papillomavirus HPV16 E6 oncoprotein similarly impairs NF-{kappa}B signaling and increases nuclear IKK? localization in human keratinocytes, suggesting a shared mechanism between mouse and human papillomaviruses. Additionally, analysis of previously published RNA sequencing data reveals that MmuPV1 E6 induces several transcriptional changes associated with increased nuclear IKK?. Together, these findings demonstrate that both MmuPV1 and HPV16 E6 disrupt NF-{kappa}B signaling in association with increased nuclear IKK? localization. This study provides the first evidence of an E6 oncoprotein interacting with and changing subcellular localization of IKK? to disrupt cellular homeostasis.

papers.title: Seasonal H1N1 influenza A virus preferentially infects a pre-existing ciliogenesis-primed secretory cell state
papers.abstract: Influenza A viruses (IAV) infect secretory and ciliated cells of the human airway epithelium , but whether all cells within one cell type are equally susceptible to infection remains unresolved. Here, single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of primary human bronchial epithelial cultures from three donors identified preferential infection of a transcriptionally distinct subpopulation of secretory cells by seasonal H1N1 IAV A/Hawaii/70/2019 . Genes upregulated in this subpopulation showed enrichment for cilium-related gene ontology terms. In an ex post facto approach, this enrichment persisted after excluding genes differentially expressed between infected and mock-treated samples, including those identified in secretory cell-specific comparisons. Single-cell analysis further revealed no significant increase in ciliogenesis scores in infected secretory cells compared to mock infected cells at 6 hours post-infection , arguing against infection-induced activation of the canonical ciliogenesis programme during the initial viral replication cycle . Collectively, these results support preferential infection of ciliogenesis-primed secretory cells and refine IAV tropism beyond cell type to encompass epithelial differentiation state.

papers.title: Structural and functional examination of Neisseria gonorrhoeae TfpC reveals a dynamic two-domain architecture required for type IV pilus function
papers.abstract: The Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Gc) Type IV pilus (T4p) is a critical apparatus for colonization and virulence. This molecular machine resides at the host-pathogen interface and mediates adherence to host cells, twitching motility, natural transformation, and resistance to oxidative agents. Previously, we identified a DUF4124 family, T4p component, TfpC. TfpC is required for full T4p elaboration, and deleting the tfpC gene reduced natural transformation competence and resulted in an under-piliated colony morphology. Our earlier models suggested TfpC is composed of an N-terminal transmembrane helix and a proline-rich disordered region followed by a C-terminal coiled-coil. Here, we used targeted structural and genetic approaches to define TfpC's molecular structure. Our new data show that TfpC's N-terminal domain forms a novel, dynamic three-stranded {beta}-sheet structure. These data indicate that the flexible disordered region acts as a linker between the N- and C-terminal domains. Functionally, we illustrate TfpC requires an acidic face within the C-terminal coiled-coil domain to mediate pilus biogenesis and function. This study characterizes a unique protein fold and family and defines the contributions of TfpC's domains to its function.
